content: In low-income settings, even within research contexts, certain challenges persist, such as managing young, HIV-positive, and malnourished individuals. The panel endorsed a decision regarding the use of diagnostic tests, but the quality of evidence was adjusted from very low to low due to consistent findings in recent studies showing that interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) have lower sensitivity compared to the tuberculin skin test (TST). The second edition of the policy on commercial serodiagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis strongly recommends against their use in individuals suspected of having active pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, regardless of HIV status. The evidence quality for these tests was deemed very low, with the risks and harms significantly outweighing any potential benefits. The panel found no new data to reconsider this recommendation but included children explicitly in the updated phrasing of the recommendation. Routine HIV testing is recommended for all patients with presumptive or diagnosed TB, including children, as part of a comprehensive diagnostic approach. This is based on strong and consistent data showing that HIV status significantly impacts TB risk, TB-related mortality, and management. However, no studies directly compare the outcomes of testing versus not testing for HIV in various endemic settings. Revised dosage recommendations for TB treatment in children were made to address the need for higher drug dosages in young children compared to older children and adults to achieve optimal serum drug levels. The recommended daily dosages are as follows: isoniazid (H) 10 mg/kg (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg/day), rifampicin (R) 15 mg/kg (range 10–20 mg/kg, maximum 600 mg/day), pyrazinamide (Z) 35 mg/kg (range 30–40 mg/kg), and ethambutol (E) 20 mg/kg (range 15–25 mg/kg). These changes are supported by recent pharmacokinetic data showing improved serum levels in young children with the updated dosages compared to the previous 2006 recommendations. However, BCG vaccination is contraindicated in individuals with impaired immunity, including HIV-positive children. For infants born to HIV-positive mothers, vaccination decisions should consider local factors such as TB prevalence, HIV prevalence, and the capacity for follow-up and early virological testing. The panel noted that the epidemiology of BCG disease has changed, with fewer infants born with HIV due to improved prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs and increased access to early antiretroviral therapy (ART). Contact screening and management for TB should prioritize children with symptoms suggestive of TB, those under five years of age, children with immunocompromising conditions (especially HIV), and contacts of multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB cases. Children under five years of age who are close contacts of TB patients and do not have active TB should receive six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) at 10 mg/kg per day (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg/day). In high HIV-prevalence settings, all household and close contacts of TB patients should be counseled and tested for HIV. For children living with HIV, six months of IPT may provide additional protection against TB in high TB-prevalence settings, even when ART is available. In medium or low TB-prevalence settings, IPT may be offered based on resource considerations. The panel recommended further research in this area and split the recommendation into two separate guidelines for high and medium/low TB-prevalence settings. Management of drug-resistant TB in children should follow the principles outlined in the 2006 guidance, with no significant changes. Children with proven or suspected pulmonary TB or tuberculous meningitis caused by MDR bacilli can be treated with a fluoroquinolone as part of an appropriate MDR-TB regimen under the supervision of an experienced clinician. Treatment outcomes for MDR-TB in children are at least as good as those in adults, and the treatment is generally well-tolerated. While no specific recommendations were made for children, the principles of infection control are relevant to all TB patients, including children.
